point.anime-nihongo: When you hear a new word in anime, look at who is saying it to whom. Words shouted at an enemy are risky. Words said to friends or teachers are often safe to use.
point.baito-keigo: For customer-service language, the shortcut is to memorize the set rephrasings: 「わかりました → かしこまりました」 (I understand), 「ちょっと → 少々」 (a little), 「すみません → 申し訳ございません」 (I'm sorry), and 「あります → ございます」 (there is; we have). These four alone will make you sound much more professional.
point.daijoubu: When you are offered something, 「大丈夫です」 usually means "No, thank you." If you do want it, say 「はい、お願いします」 (Yes, please).
point.itami-onomatopoeia: Onomatopoeia for pain and bodily sensations is used in the pattern 「〜が + onomatopoeia + 痛いです／します」. Add 「痛いです」 (it hurts) for pain, and 「します」 (I feel ...) for sensations other than pain: ムカムカ (queasy), ゾクゾク (shivery), and クラクラ (dizzy).
point.kanji-himitsu-01: When you come across a kanji you don't know, first try breaking it into its parts. You can often guess the meaning of the kanji from the meanings of its parts.
point.kanji-himitsu-02: For kanji with many readings, the shortcut is to learn them as whole words. Instead of memorizing a single kanji, learn it in words such as 「なまビール」 (draft beer), 「いっしょう」 (one's whole life), and 「しばふ」 (lawn).
point.kazoekata: If you are not sure how to count something, use 「1つ、2つ」 (hitotsu, futatsu) or 「1個、2個」 (ikko, niko), and you will be understood for most things. Then switch to the correct counters little by little.
point.kimochi-onomatopoeia: Many onomatopoeia for feelings become verbs when you add 「〜する」 (to do): 「ワクワクする」 (to be excited), 「ドキドキした」 (my heart was pounding), 「ホッとしました」 (I felt relieved). Try using them in sentences, and you will remember them quickly.
point.konbini-nihongo: 「大丈夫です」 is an all-purpose phrase that gently conveys "No, thank you." However, it can sometimes be hard to tell whether you mean "yes" or "no." If you say it while lightly waving your hand, the meaning "No, thank you" will come across clearly.
point.nihon-ichi: When you learn a "number one in Japan," it is a good idea to learn number two along with it. "Do you know number one? Then what about number two?" makes a good conversation topic with Japanese people.
point.sensei-message: Write a message to your teacher in the order "name → what you need to say → thanks." It is enough just to change the words you use with friends into their polite forms.
point.sumimasen: At the center of 「すみません」 is the feeling "I have put a burden on you." Its three uses — apologizing, thanking, and getting someone's attention — all come from this feeling.
point.todofuken-hint: It is a good idea to learn each prefecture as a set of "location, food, and festival." When the conversation turns to where someone is from, being able to say 「〇〇が有名ですよね」 ("〇〇 is famous there, isn't it?") will make the conversation lively.
point.umi-nai-ken: As in 「海なし県」 (landlocked prefecture; literally "prefecture without sea"), you can make words meaning "without ..." with the pattern "noun + なし". Expressions such as 「家族なし」 (no family), 「予定なし」 (no plans), and 「問題なし」 (no problem) are often used in notes and conversation.
point.yabai: At the core of 「やばい」 is the sense of "going beyond the normal range." Whether that is in a positive or a negative direction is decided by the context.
point.yoroshiku: At the center of 「よろしくお願いします」 is the feeling "I trust you and leave it to you." What exactly you are asking for is decided by the situation.
